# Insecure Deserialization in Plain English: When Bytes Become Code

Insecure deserialization is not a niche CVE flavor. It is what happens when your app rebuilds objects from bytes it should not trust. Serialization turns a live object into a stream (file, cookie, HTTP body, queue message). Deserialization does the reverse: it reads those bytes and constructs objects again. Native Java serialization — `ObjectOutputStream` out, `ObjectInputStream.readObject()` in — does more than restore field values. It can run constructor logic, custom `readObject` methods, and class-loading decisions while the stream is still being read. If an attacker controls the stream, that machinery becomes their interpreter.

OWASP maps this under [A08:2025 Software or Data Integrity Failures](https://owasp.org/Top10/2025/A08_2025-Software_or_Data_Integrity_Failures/) (CWE-502: Deserialization of Untrusted Data). The integrity failure is simple: you treated attacker-shaped bytes as a trusted object graph. Impacts range from denial of service to privilege abuse to remote code execution, depending on what classes are on the classpath and what those classes do when reconstructed.

## What “gadget” means without the jargon

You do not need a zero-day in `ObjectInputStream` for this to bite. Researchers chain ordinary classes already on your classpath — “gadgets” — whose `readObject`, `readResolve`, or related magic methods do something powerful with field values the attacker chose. The cast after `readObject()` does not help: by the time you write `(AcmeObject) ois.readObject()`, the dangerous work may already have run. OWASP’s community write-up on [deserialization of untrusted data](https://owasp.org/www-community/vulnerabilities/Deserialization_of_untrusted_data) is blunt about that timing.

Java streams often leave fingerprints if you know where to look. The [OWASP Deserialization Cheat Sheet](https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Deserialization_Cheat_Sheet.html) calls out hex magic `AC ED 00 05`, Base64 that starts with `rO0`, and `Content-Type: application/x-java-serialized-object`. Those are hunting signals for leftover remoting, session blobs, or “temporary” binary APIs — not proof by themselves, but enough to start a code search.

## Filters help; they are not on by default

JDK 9+ shipped serialization filtering ([JEP 290](https://openjdk.org/jeps/290); Oracle’s current guide is [Java Serialization Filters](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/core/java-serialization-filters.html)). You can set a JVM-wide pattern filter with `jdk.serialFilter`, or attach a stream-specific `ObjectInputFilter` before you read. Filters can allow or reject classes and packages, and they can cap array length, graph depth, reference count, and stream size.

Oracle’s docs are equally clear on the trap: **a serialization filter is not enabled by default.** No property, no Security Property, no `ObjectInputFilter` on the stream means no filtering. An allowlist (only the classes you expect) is safer than a denylist of yesterday’s gadgets. OWASP’s cheat sheet still recommends hardening `ObjectInputStream` (override `resolveClass`, or use a validating subclass) when you must keep native serialization at all — and it still opens with the better answer: prefer data-only formats.

## Spring Boot and Angular: where this actually lives in a strangler

This bug is almost always **server-side Java**. Your Angular SPA does not deserialize `ObjectInputStream`. What the SPA *does* change is which old server paths stay reachable.

In a Java 8 monolith being strangled toward Spring Boot APIs plus Angular, the risky leftovers look like:

- Servlets or controllers that do `new ObjectInputStream(request.getInputStream()).readObject()`
- Session or cookie blobs that round-trip Java-serialized state
- Legacy remoting: RMI, JMS message bodies, or Spring’s old HTTP Invoker

Spring Framework’s own Javadoc for [`HttpInvokerServiceExporter`](https://docs.spring.io/spring-framework/docs/5.3.x/javadoc-api/org/springframework/remoting/httpinvoker/HttpInvokerServiceExporter.html) (deprecated as of 5.3 while serialization-based remoting was phased out) warns explicitly: manipulated input streams can lead to unwanted code execution during deserialization; do not expose HTTP invoker endpoints to untrusted clients; prefer another message format such as JSON. That is the product truth for strangler work — replace the binary remoting edge with a JSON/REST (or similar) contract when you cut a section over, instead of keeping the invoker “just for the old clients.”

Jackson, XStream, SnakeYAML, and friends have their own footguns when type metadata or polymorphic typing lets the payload pick the class. OWASP’s cheat sheet separates libraries that are safe by default from those that need strict config. JSON over the wire is still the right direction for a Spring Boot + Angular cutover; turn off “deserialize any `@type`” style features and keep DTOs boring.

## What to do in a Java / Spring / Angular / GitLab CI shop

1. **Prefer not to deserialize untrusted native Java streams.** Replace section-by-section with Spring Boot controllers that accept JSON DTOs and an Angular client that never sends `rO0…` blobs. Strangler replacement removes attack surface; an in-place JDK bump does not.
2. **Inventory sinks before you “harden later.”** Search for `ObjectInputStream`, `readObject`, `readUnshared`, `Serializable` on request/session paths, HTTP Invoker exporters, and queue consumers. Treat every hit as a ticket with an owner.
3. **If a binary edge must stay for a release, put an allowlist filter in front of it.** Use `ObjectInputFilter` / `jdk.serialFilter` with an explicit allowlist of expected types plus size/depth limits. Do not ship “filter TBD.”
4. **Sign or HMAC any serialized blob that still crosses a trust boundary**, and reject streams that fail the check before you deserialize — OWASP A08’s prevention guidance for unsigned serialized data from untrusted clients.
5. **Kill legacy remoting on the cutover checklist.** When a monolith slice moves to Spring Boot 3 / Framework 6-era stacks, serialization-based HTTP Invoker is already gone from the framework; do not reintroduce equivalent `ObjectInputStream` endpoints by hand.
6. **Wire detection into GitLab CI you already run.** Fail SAST / custom grep jobs on new `ObjectInputStream` + untrusted `InputStream` patterns the same way you fail on secret leaks. Add a smoke test that rejects a truncated `rO0` / `AC ED` probe on any endpoint that used to accept Java serialization.

## The short version

Insecure deserialization means your server rebuilt an object graph from bytes an attacker shaped — and Java’s native serializer can run code while it does that. OWASP groups it under software/data integrity failures. Fix it by not accepting untrusted Java-serialized streams: move strangler edges to JSON DTOs, allowlist-filter anything that must remain, drop HTTP Invoker / similar remoting, and keep Angular on boring REST contracts. Filters and validating streams are seatbelts for the migration window — not a reason to keep binary object graphs on the public edge.
chris_take_options: A: The counterintuitive failure mode in strangler shops is not “we forgot ObjectInputFilter” — it is keeping one “compatibility” HTTP Invoker or session-serialized cookie for the last thick client, because that single path keeps the entire gadget-rich classpath reachable from the internet while the Angular apps look modern.

B: Pick one concrete gate this quarter: any MR that adds or retains ObjectInputStream.readObject / readUnshared on a request, session, or queue consumer must ship a linked allowlist ObjectInputFilter (or jdk.serialFilter pattern) and a CI grep that fails new sinks without a suppressions file owner — no filter, no merge.

C: The lived AppSec trade-off is ugly: a strict allowlist will break an undocumented internal tool that stuffed custom Serializable types into JMS before it stops a real exploit, so run the filter in reject-log / stage first for one sprint, expand the allowlist from real traffic, then enforce — waiting for a perfect inventory is how the binary edge stays forever.
